stories.title: Britain, EU set to agree to reset but divisions persist
stories.summary: Britain and the European Union are set to agree on easing food trade and youth mobility in a reset of ties at a summit that is also likely to expose lingering divisions and question marks over the long-term future of their relationship. A decade after Britain voted to leave the now 27-nation bloc, rancour over the divorce has faded and both sides have recognised the need for a closer alliance in a world order upset by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, US tariffs, Chinese control of critical minerals and war in Iran. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is prepared to walk away from a deal if it is not in Britain's interests, as negotiations went down to the wire ahead of his meeting with EU leaders in Brussels. Mr Burnham said he was determined to secure "the best deal for Britain" as he talked up the prospect of lower food prices, reduced costs for businesses and stronger co-operation on tackling illegal migration. At the summit, postponed from July following the resignation of Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer, the two sides aim to address a small part of those losses with a package of agreements. The most significant would allow cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1 billion (€6.09bn) per year to its economy.

stories.title: Housing shortage can trap women in abusive homes - report
stories.summary: A new report by the National Women's Council says intimate partner violence remains one of the most significant threats to women’s safety in Ireland. The report also says that leaving a violent situation can be the most dangerous time, and can also raise other issues, particularly finding somewhere else to live. Many victim-survivors of domestic abuse face a choice between staying in a potentially dangerous situation or leaving and becoming homeless, the report finds. "These are two crises that are so interlinked and intertwined." "Women are now in a situation where they're either forced to stay in a housing situation that is potentially unsafe right up to life-threatening, or they can flee the home and potentially risk homelessness, because unfortunately there aren't too many places for women to go," she said. She said a worrying statistic is that gardaí reported "that they dealt with 1,000 incidents of domestic abuse every week last year [2025]."

stories.title: UK retail sales rise 0.7% in October, beating forecasts
stories.summary: British retail sales volumes unexpectedly rose 0.7% in October compared with September, official figures show today. Economists polled by Reuters had a median forecast that sales volumes would be unchanged on the month. UK consumer sentiment had fallen sharply in October, according to Britain's longest-running measure of this, as rising fuel bills and borrowing costs squeezed households, although November data showed ⁠a small recovery. Consumer price inflation rose to a one-year high of 3.6% in October and the Bank of England forecast it would reach close to 5% in the middle of next ‌year when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years ⁠this month. However, overall economic growth has ‌been stronger than expected this year and recent updates from ⁠major ‌British retailers have been mixed. Clothing and food retailer Marks & Spencer said recent trading had been solid and it entered the Christmas period ⁠with momentum, while Primark and Next highlighted a pickup in ⁠sales in October when the weather turned colder.

stories.title: No truce on energy facility attacks, says Putin
stories.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said there will be no agreements to halt attacks on sea and energy facilities after Ukrainian strikes on Crimean Bridge. Mr Putin also said Russia would retaliate following the strikes on the bridge linking Russia ⁠and Crimea. Speaking in the Chinese city of Shenzhen after talks with the leaders of China and the US, he made the comments after Ukraine struck the bridge for the third time in a week, forcing a brief suspension of train services. The Russian president, visibly angry, said he had initially asked his Security Council to consider a possible agreement to halt attacks at sea and on energy facilities. "But after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will be no agreements. We will respond to these strikes," he said. "And I want everyone to know this: I believe our response will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge."

stories.title: Record income for Mayo GAA after All-Ireland winning year
stories.summary: Mayo GAA's sensational 2026 was not confined to the pitch as the Connacht county has welcomed record income and profits off the back of a first All-Ireland SFC title since 1951. Mayo's 2026 financial report, covering 12 months to the end of September, makes for fine reading for the county with net profits seeing a massive rise of 212% to €1.42m off revenue of €6.3m. It leaves Mayo in rude financial health with a balance sheet that stands at €6.8m at year-end, including €3.3m of cash reserves. As a result, all clubs in the county are set to receive a €2,500 appreciation grant while a 'One Mayo' initiative will be launched next year to investigate further ways to offer financial support to clubs from fundraising proceeds. Commercial income (€1.74m), fundraising income (€1.49m), gate receipts and matchday income (€800,000) were also up on the previous year, significantly so for the first two. Total income from the GAA's central council, the Allianz Football League and provincial allocations amounted to €1.6m in 2026 – a 43% increase on the previous year.

stories.title: The charts and streaming playlists are full of old music. Why?
stories.summary: The music industry has changed, and so have people's listening habits, and as a result the charts are full of old music. Why? It’s complicated, Kate Demolder writes. Remember when Spotify told you your listening age was 75? Well, it turns out, you’re not alone. Despite some 150,000 tracks being added to streaming services every day, pretty much all of us are choosing to listen to old music. According to independent entertainment data and analytics company Luminate, older music – defined as tracks released more than 18 months ago – has swelled to roughly 70% of U.S. music consumption. Closer to home, the charts are displaying the same: In the Irish charts on the week of publication, Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s "Rein Me In", released February 2025, joins Jade Thirlwall’s 2024 hit "Angel of My Dreams" and Michael Jackson’s 1982 megasmash "Thriller" in the top 20, while Kingfishr’s "Killeagh" from December 2024, and Kings of Leon’s 2013 hit "Wait For Me" round out the top 25. Though some may laugh at the idea of 18-month-old tracks being hailed as old, the entire music business model is built on the promotion of new songs. As an arts writer, I receive dozens of emails a week from promoters looking to get their artists’ newest record some attention, and yet, few appear to be breaking through. Indeed, consumer interest in listening to older music has been increasing in recent years, like in the UK, where hits like Jackson’s "Billie Jean" and Fleetwood Mac’s "Dreams" are not only reentering the albums chart, but joining eighteen of the year's top 20 tracks as pieces of music that have been released either 12 months ago or earlier. In the US, music listeners aged 13 to 24 – the most important and targeted audience in the industry – are getting more active in embracing music from the 1990s or earlier. This hasn’t happened by accident, says Dr Michael Murphy, an IADT lecturer with expertise in the music industry. "This is the way the music industry is going. The most brilliant unseen marketing concentration is ensuring that a lot of people are exposed to the same thing at the same time, meaning taste pathways are smoothed out to make gigs and albums social events that people run the risk of missing out on if they’re not involved." Murphy cites the recent addition of Kate Bush’s "Running Up That Hill" – a 1985 hit that was recently featured in an episode of Netflix’s hit show Stranger Things – to the number one slot in the charts as an example. "As much as I love that song, I remember thinking at the time that that was a disaster for music," he says. "Because what that did was eliminate the number one position in that week for a new band, who probably worked their socks off to release their own material." Success was always short-lived in the music business, but now new songs – genuine hits among them – can pass unnoticed by much of the population. In fact, the audience seems to be embracing the hits of decades past instead. (This much can be seen from Grammys interest, which according to The Hollywood Reporter has gone from 17.09 million viewers in 2024 to 14.41 million viewers in 2026.) Of course, the mechanics of new music breaking through today are very different. Thanks to streaming, the algorithms that power playlists are programmed to keep users on the app, which means feeding them music that triggers immediate familiarity rather than challenging them with the unfamiliar. If a listener skips a new track, the algorithm registers a failure. As such, catalogue music – defined by the industry as any track older than 18 months – presents zero risk. "The 'superstar economy’ is a term that’s going around," Dr Murphy adds. "It’s when the entire market is focused on a very small group of artists, which is a very dangerous moment for music indeed. Think about it: how many people do you know have gone to a Taylor Swift or Oasis gig in recent years? And then contrast that with how many people have gone to an upstairs gig in Whelans in the past 12 months?" The TikTokification of music, then – that music these days must have a 15-second clip that has the capacity to go viral on TikTok for it to succeed – now dictates who’s on top, and is why a 1975 Fleetwood Mac b-side, which was repopularised by a skating TikTok creator who uses it as his videos’ score, is entering the charts in the same way as a brand-new release. When these archival tracks go viral, millions of Gen Z and Millennial users migrate to streaming apps to listen to the full version, sending decades-old music straight back into the official Top 40 alongside contemporary releases. "It presents a tricky conundrum for new acts," Colm Hanley, Managing Director of AIM Ireland, the trade body for Ireland’s independent music sector, says. "With streaming, there are more opportunities in the form of soundtracks for artists to break through. But, when those opportunities are given to already established acts like Kate Bush, you can;t help but think to yourself, could this have been an opportunity for a new act?"

stories.title: Rooney recalls toll of Wagatha Christie case on wife
stories.summary: Wayne Rooney told his I'm a Celebrity campmates how "horrible" it was for his wife Coleen to go through a libel battle with Rebekah Vardy. Last year, a court ruled that Rebekah Vardy had to pay Coleen Rooney at least £1.4 million (€1.6 million) in legal costs. Their libel battle kicked off after Coleen posted on social media in 2019 that Vardy’s Instagram account was responsible for leaking information about her to The Sun newspaper. Last year a judge ordered Rebekah pay Coleen at least £1.4 million (€1.6 million) in legal costs following their high-profile court case. Former footballer Wayne is currently competing on the latest season of I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! On Thursday night’s episode his fellow campmate, comedian Leigh Francis, told Wayne that before going into camp he had watched a TV series based on the Wagatha Christie case.

stories.title: The best festive sambos & treats to try in Dublin this Christmas
stories.summary: Christmas is a time for truly exceptional things that seem to take on even more glow with each passing year. Family traditions, twinkling lights and ribboned gifts, quality time with friends and family. The list goes on. But almost all of them pale against that one special festive delight: the Christmas sambo. Thankfully, cafes up and down the country have not only nailed the annual treat but managed to find ever more ways to reinvent a downright perfect classic. From varieties of bread and lashings of richly flavoured sauces, to surprising additions and even a Christmas dinner-inspired pastry, there are some true gems out there to try this year. We've rounded up our favourites nice and early, to give you plenty of time to sample them all. Is it controversial to start with a Christmas pastry? Perhaps, but this one is what we've been wishing for all year. The extraordinarily talents chefs at Elliots are serving up a Christmas Pain Suisse, a technical marvel of a cross laminated croissant filled with baked Salters ham, braised turkey crown, Brie de Meaux and the last of the summers Wicklow raspberry preserve, all topped with a sourdough and crispy sage stuffing. Having bewitched sambo lovers all summer with their specials, Loverboy is branching out into festive versions, offering an indulgent creation filled with roast turkey, roast ham, stuffing, brie, cranberry sauce, mustard mayo and house onion gravy toasted on ciabatta. There is a vegetarian option also available!

stories.title: Over 250,000 taken off hospital waiting lists since 2024
stories.summary: Over a quarter of a million people have been taken off hospital waiting lists since January 2024 because they failed to respond to validation forms sent by post. These are forms that check whether patients are available to attend a hospital appointment or if they wish to be removed from the waiting list. So far this year, 77,720 people have been removed for not responding to the forms. This compares with 96,880 last year, and 90,345 people in 2024. The data was supplied to Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín in a parliamentary question. "Nearly 265,000 patients have been taken off hospital waiting lists simply because they did not respond to correspondence," he said.

stories.title: Anthropic's debut tests Wall Street's faith in AI boom
stories.summary: Anthropic notched a valuation of about $2 trillion in its Nasdaq debut yesterday, edging past SpaceX's June listing and capping a turbulent stretch for the AI sector that tested Wall Street's appetite for the technology. The early exuberance faded, however, signaling volatility ahead as investors locked in quick gains and the main indexes retreated amid renewed jitters over the sector's outlook. Shares of the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company opened at $111.50, which was 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 set on Wednesday. But the stock pared gains and ended the day at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. Anthropic's fully diluted $2 trillion valuation includes stock options and restricted stock units that the company has promised employees but which have not been vested into actual shares. Based on Anthropic's outstanding shares, the company's value reached as much as $1.5 trillion yesterday, on a par with Tesla.

stories.title: Van der Flier: 'These are the games you want to play in'
stories.summary: Josh van der Flier admits Ireland will have to get "everything" right if they are to turn over the world champions South Africa in Dublin on Saturday. Ireland host the Springboks in their final home game of the inaugural Nations Championship, with Andy Farrell's side knowing they will likely need to win if they are to finish in the top two of the northern hemisphere table. The week leading up to this game has been dogged by controversy, with South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus given a six-game ban following comments he made about match officials, while Ireland's Sam Prendergast avoided a potential suspension after he was cited for an alleged hip-drop tackle against Fiji. But Van der Flier is ignoring the chaos around this game, and setting his sights only on the rugby. "I can only speak for myself really, but I pretty much have everything to do with rugby blocked on my phone," the Ireland flanker said of the storm that has been brewing in recent days. "I don't look at any of the stuff. There's a quote I like from John Wooden, which is: 'Don't let praise or criticism get to you. It's a weakness to get caught up in either one'.

stories.title: Poison Ink: the anonymous letters terrorising a Dublin community
stories.summary: Once upon a time in North Dublin, someone typed out a note: "Number 36 are dangerous people with a profile of harming children, please keep your distance and keep children away from them to avoid harm." This statement, while entirely false, was part of a five-year campaign of terror that would upend the victims' faith in their community leaving them fearing for their safety and questioning who they could trust. The victims of this crime had no idea who was committing this offence, when they would strike next or if their stalking would intensify. What they did know was that this shadowy figure was watching them and knew exactly where they lived… I realise this all sounds alarmingly like an Agatha Christie novel from the 1920s, but these were real people, and this story began in 2018. Publishing this Friday, episode one covers the early days of this war by pen as two unsuspecting families are drawn into an unimaginable nightmare by an anonymous entity. Narrated by writer Sarah Maria Griffin, once the target of a stalker herself, she brings an emotive yet reassuring tone to the story, perhaps owing to the fact that she can empathise with the victims.

stories.title: You Can See Everything: the slipperiest film of 2026
stories.summary: Chances are, you've heard plenty about You Can See Everything already, and you'll be hearing a lot more as this near-three-hour documentary bosses the Irish box office and conversations in the weeks ahead. Screenings are already sold out and there's talk of a Best Picture Oscar nomination - a first for a documentary. Three and a half years after her imprisonment for a near-half-billion fraud, Theranos founder and CEO Elizabeth Holmes continues to fascinate. Her infamy has grown since 2023. Holmes' invention, The Edison, was billed - by her - as "the iPod of healthcare", a device to run hundreds of tests with a drop of blood. She was found guilty on four counts of defrauding investors but not guilty of defrauding patients. Roughly a month before her incarceration, Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invited directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into their home because, as Evans puts it on screen, Holmes had been "turned into this monster" and "nobody knows who she is". What follows plays like a thriller, belies its almost three-hour running time, and leaves you constantly trying to pin down what you've just watched. How Holmes presents herself to Fielder, Oppenheim, and us is at odds with the public perception, and Fielder appears increasingly conflicted about his subject as the clock ticks down to the start of Holmes' sentence. How much sympathy does Holmes deserve as a mother about to go to prison? Could a CEO really be this guileless? Is this one of the best performances in screen history? These are just some of the questions guaranteed to go through your head - and you'll have plenty of others.

stories.title: Irish folklore-inspired look wins at sustainable fashion comp
stories.summary: A design celebrating Irish folklore was named the winner of Enable Ireland's nationwide sustainable fashion competition, The Final Find 2026. Taking place at The Pillar Room in Dublin on Wednesday 18 November, and hosted by content creator Katrina Carroll and Paria Hilton, the Brand and Comms Director of Dublin Independent Fashion Week, the competition's glittering grand finale celebrated circular fashion, creativity and sustainability, as well as spotlighting vital disability services. Now in its second year, the competition saw a host of aspiring designers, stylists, upcyclers and fashionistas transform charity shop finds into runway-worthy looks. Each contestant received a 'mystery bag' of items from Enable Ireland charity shops and were tasked with creating runway-worthy looks from the items and their own clothing and accessories. The dazzling creations showcased just how much textiles and clothing can be repurposed and reused to create iconic looks in a myriad of jaw-dropping styles. Contestants from Cork, Waterford, Limerick, Kilkenny, and Dublin came together with designs inspired by everything from 1960's chic to avant-garde, maximalist and military styles. The judging panel on the night consisted of Dearbhla Lovett, an Activations Executive with IMAGE and freelance Brand Creative Strategist, Disability Inclusion Advocate Mikey O'Doherty, and Enable Ireland Head of Commercial, Oonagh O’Connor. The top prize went to Jessica Rodrigues, a multidisciplinary artist from Smithfield, Dublin.

stories.title: Relatives of Omagh bombing victims 'beyond despair'
stories.summary: A relative and friend of two young Donegal schoolboys killed in the Omagh bombing has said the Irish Government has a duty to hold a public inquiry into their deaths. Oran Doherty, aged eight, and 12-year-old Shaun McLaughlin, both from Buncrana, were among the 29 people killed in the attack by dissident republicans on 15 August 1998. They went to the same school and lived in the same street, just a short distance from the cemetery where they are buried, side by side. They were on a school trip together when their young lives were ended by the car bomb that ripped through Omagh. A UK inquiry being held in Belfast has heard a claim that an agent working for An Garda Síochána was part of the team that brought the bomb to the town on that sunny August afternoon. The claim was made by retired chief superintendent Norman Baxter, who led the PSNI investigation into the attack.

stories.title: BASF ends pursuit of Evonik as $12 billion bid rejected
stories.summary: German chemicals group BASF has abandoned its pursuit of Evonik, saying that its smaller rival remained unwilling to engage despite the prospect of a further increase to its takeover offer. "The executive board of Evonik has not shown meaningful engagement," even though BASF had indicated it was considering a further "moderate increase" of its offer, BASF said in a statement. "BASF's assessment of Evonik's standalone prospects and associated risks did not provide sufficient grounds to justify a higher valuation," it added. Evonik interim CEO Claus Rettig said his company could now focus all of its energy on independent development. "This removes a source of uncertainty for our employees," he said in an emailed statement. BASF first approached Evonik in September and later raised its offer to €11.2 billion, or €24 per share, after Evonik rejected its initial proposal.

stories.summary: Japanese soccer official Kozo Tashima said that the handling of Folarin Balogun's red card at the World Cup was what prompted him to run for the role of FIFA president against Gianni Infantino. FIFA suspended forward Balogun's ⁠automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after US President Donald Trump said he had personally asked President Infantino to review the sanction. The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, fuelled opposition to Infantino's reelection as president. Tashima said he wanted to restore trust in FIFA, drawing parallels with 2016, when Infantino took charge after a corruption scandal. "Ten years ago something similar happened, and Mr Infantino became president to reform and improve things," the Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president told a press conference. "He has certainly done wonderful things. But in this year, 2026, 10 years later, events have occurred that ignored governance.

stories.title: Thomas Markle ruled fit for child sex abuse images trial
stories.summary: Thomas Markle, who has been accused of possessing child sex abuse material including images of himself with naked young girls, has been ruled competent to stand trial in the US following a psychiatric assessment. The doctor who carried out the evaluation said, in her opinion, Mr Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, was "malingering because he is exaggerating a lack of recall or understanding of the charges in order to avoid criminal prosecution". The examination was ordered by a Florida judge following his arrest earlier this month. After initially being released on conditional bail, the 82 year old was taken back into custody just days later after removing his electronic monitoring tag. The 16-page report on Mr Markle was compiled by Dr Amie Gerodimos, an assistant professor at the department of psychiatry and behavioural neurosciences at the University of South Florida. She carried out her forensic psychiatric interview of Markle Sr in the medical unit at Pinellas County Jail, on 12 November.

stories.title: O'Connor hoping to help Martin's drive on after injury
stories.summary: Imagine suffering two cruciate knee ligament injuries in 14 months. Imagine being the third member of your family to suffer that double blow. Imagine all four siblings having done it once. You might wonder if there is a hex on the household but that's not the way the O’Connors roll. Ciara O’Connor knuckled down and the St Martin’s and Wexford sharpshooter returned for the third group game of the latest club championship. She played her first full game in the semi-final and starred as Martins beat Glynn Barntown in the decider. Now, thanks in no small part to O’Connor’s 10 points against Offaly champions Shinrone in the AIB Leinster semi-final, they are back in a provincial final, against Dicksboro, at Chadwicks Wexford Park on Sunday (3.30pm). The Kilkenny exemplars, current champions, beat them in the 2023 semi-final and went on to secure All-Ireland garlands. This year is the first time Martin’s have been county champions since. The Piercestown/Murrintown contingent had themselves been in the All-Ireland final in 2019, when Slaughtneil completed a remarkable three-in-a-row. That was the era when the competition straddled Christmas and they reached the provincial decider most recently towards the end of that same year, losing by two points to St Vincent’s.

stories.title: ICJ ruling on Myanmar hailed as 'milestone' for Rohingya
stories.summary: The ruling by the International Court of Justice that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority is a "milestone", a member of the Rohingya community living in Ireland has said. The court yesterday laid out evidence of Myanmar's atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in western Rakhine state. Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed "widespread sexual violence" against women and "extreme violence" against children, the court's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, said. Hichael Rashid left Myanmar, formally known as Burma, 21 years ago and now lives in Carlow. Mr Rashid said that action against the Rohingya did not begin in 2017, saying that "life in Burma has been a living hell because we have been stripped of citizenship by [the] 1982 citizenship law, even though my parents and grandparents were citizens of Burma." He added: "And then we have been stripped of everything, basic human rights, freedom of education, healthcare, freedom of moment, access to livelihood and all the things."

stories.title: Farrell backs 'world class' Sheehan to make back row mark
stories.summary: Andy Farrell is backing Dan Sheehan to take his move into the back row "in his stride" ahead of Saturday's meeting with South Africa. The Ireland head coach has taken a page straight out of the Springbok playbook by testing his captain out in the back row, with Sheehan lining out at number 8 for just the second time in his career. The Leinster man was trialled in the back row for his province against Munster in the BKT United Rugby Championship last month, but faces a step up in class on Saturday when he does it against the best team in the world. "Nothing seems to really surprise you with Dan," Farrell said after naming his side for Saturday's Nations Championship clash at Aviva Stadium. "He's very cool, calm and collected; there's no arrogance there whatsoever. Things don't bother him, so he takes it all in his stride, fully confident in his own ability. "I think most people would agree that he's a world-class player. He's not just good throwing the ball in or scrummaging, his point of difference is around the field and how he plays the game, ball in hand or defensively, running lines and all of that, and that is suited to number eight."

stories.title: Russian missiles strikes target key bridges in Kyiv
stories.summary: A Russian ballistic missile attack hit three bridges on Kyiv's Dnipro River and killed three people, the city's mayor said, in the biggest strikes on routes connecting the left and right banks of Ukraine's capital since the start of the war. The missiles hit the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi Bridge crossing, and the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or traffic restrictions in the city of some 3 million people commuting over six main bridges. Three people were killed and around 15 others were injured, he added. The strikes, which also caused fires and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings, come as Russian President Vladimir Putin promised to hit back hard after Ukraine hit the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week. Five people were also injured in the Dnipropetrovsk region after drones hit apartment buildings, and four others wounded in Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-biggest city, after Russian drones hit a hospital. One person was wounded in a drone attack on a tram in Zaporizhzhia, local officials said on Telegram.

stories.summary: CJ Stroud threw for three touchdowns as the Houston Texans' defence dominated the Indianapolis Colts in a 26-3 victory. It was one-way traffic from there, as Stroud connected with Nico Collins, Kayshon Boutte and Marlin Klein to propel Houston to their first home win of the season. Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was held to just 144 yards and an interception as Indianapolis fell to a 3-8 record on the season.

stories.title: Parents Council raises concern over school transport fees
stories.summary: The National Parents Council has expressed concern over planned hikes in school transport fees from September, adding that it only learned of the proposal yesterday, despite the measure being contained in last month's Budget. The council said it will talk to parents about the measures over the coming days. Fares had been reduced as a cost-of-living measure in 2022, but will return to levels last seen for the 2021/22 academic year from next September. Under the changes, the annual charge for school transport for post-primary pupils is to rise from €100 to €350 for the 2027/2028 academic year. The Labour Party has criticised what it says is a 250% increase in fees while Sinn Féin has asked for the issue to be investigated by the Dáil's Public Accounts Committee. However, the Government argues that the current level of charges was only ever a temporary measure, and that the new fee structure will lead to a more efficient school transport scheme.

stories.title: Adeleke parts company with 'Coach Flo', making UCLA move
stories.summary: Rhasidat Adeleke has announced that she is leaving the University of Texas and parting company with coach Edrick Floreal, to move to the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). The Dublin sprinter joined 'Coach Flo's' training group at the University of Texas in 2021, where he encouraged her to focus on the 400m, despite her initial uncertainty about moving up from shorter sprint distances. Under the tutelage of Floreal, Adeleke won the 2023 NCAA Outdoor 400m title in a record-breaking 49.20, two NCAA 4x100m relay titles in 2022 and 2023, and silver in the 2023 NCAA Indoor 400m. She also shone on the international stage for Ireland in that period, finishing fourth in the 400m at the 2023 World Championships and the 2024 Paris Olympics. She won European 400m silver in 2024, set an Irish record of 49.07 seconds, and helped Ireland win mixed 4x400m European gold. Adeleke will now link up with coach Joanna Hayes at UCLA, with Los Angeles the host city for the 2028 Olympic Games. Hayes is a former elite hurdler and Olympic champion and competed at UCLA as an hugely successful athlete.

stories.title: Taoiseach to meet with CUH chief executive on Monday
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin is due to meet the Chief Executive of Cork University Hospital on Monday amid ongoing controversy around the institution. A bitter row has developed between the HSE and medics at CUH after CUH CEO Jennifer Kearney warned the HSE in August how a shortfall of 1,000 staff meant the hospital would not be safe going into winter. A spokesperson for Mr Martin said: "The Taoiseach is due to meet the CEO, senior management of CUH and HSE officials on Monday". CUH is in Mr Martin's Dáil constituency of Cork South-Central, but he has rejected calls for an independent assessment of staffing levels at the Wilton facility. On Wednesday, HSE Chief Executive Anne O'Connor told the Oireachtas Committee on Health that she had not spoken to Ms Kearney since September despite the ongoing issues at CUH. It is understood Ms O'Connor may also visit the hospital to meet management and staff next Monday.

stories.title: Delay reporting UN convoy separation, Rooney inquest told

stories.title: Fiona the hippo dies in US after swallowing visitor's hat
stories.summary: A hippo has died after swallowing a visitor's hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure at a zoo in the US. The hippo, named Fiona, became a global sensation after being born prematurely at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017. "It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. The zoo said on Monday that the hippo was undergoing care around the clock after swallowing the hat more than a week ago. Before she died, veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said. They even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move things along through her digestive tract.

stories.title: Mayo set for blockbuster Connacht opener with Roscommon
stories.summary: The 2027 Connacht SFC is set for a blockbuster opener as All-Ireland champions Mayo were drawn against provincial holders Roscommon. It will be the first time in 25 years that a provincial game in the western province will feature an All-Ireland champion facing off against a Connacht champion, Sam Maguire holders Galway flattening Nestor Cup holders Roscommon on that occasion with Alan Kerins finding the net twice in 2002. It was the only one of three quarter-final pairings drawn with Sligo's trip to New York and Leitrim’s visit to London already pre-determined. However, it was the semi-final draw that could have implications on next year’s Allianz League and provincial championships. New York, Sligo, London and Leitrim are all on one side of the draw, ensuring that one Division 3 or 4 team is guaranteed to make the All-Ireland series. At present the impact is minimal on Division 2 but the side that emerges from that quartet, along with Wicklow, will supersede the two promoted sides from Division 3 who would be ranked 15th and 16th in the league standings, so they will need to find another route to Sam.

stories.title: Woods set to design new golf course in Northern Ireland
stories.summary: Tiger Woods has confirmed he will design the first championship-standard links golf course built in Northern Ireland for more than 100 years, describing the project as a "special opportunity". Reports linking the 15-time major champion with the proposed £30 million (€35.8m) course at Bellarena on the north-west coast between Limavady and Coleraine had been circulating for several weeks ahead of Thursday's official announcement. "Northern Ireland is home to some of the greatest links golf in the world, and building one on the Causeway Coast is a special opportunity for our team," said Woods. "We want Bellarena to feel as though it has always been part of this coastline, with a course that challenges the best players and is fun for everyone who plays it." Hospitality group Galgorm Collection is building the course, with construction set to get under way next year if the required planning approvals are secured. The company already owns and runs the championship parkland course at Galgorm Castle in Ballymena and a course at Roe Valley in Limavady.
